page.text:
While the natural numbers support unrestricted addition and multiplication,
they suffer from an algebraic defect: the lack of additive inverses. An
equation as elementary as $x + 5 = 3$ possesses no solution in
$\mathbb{N}$; subtraction is only a partial, conditional operation.

The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ resolve this asymmetry by adjoining negative
numbers, completing the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{N}, +)$ into an
abelian group $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$. The classical construction—an instance
of the Grothendieck group completion—represents each integer as a formal
difference of two natural numbers, where the pair $(n, m) \in \mathbb{N}
\times \mathbb{N}$ intuitively denotes $n - m$. Identifying pairs that
represent the same difference yields an equivalence relation on $\mathbb{N}
\times \mathbb{N}$, whose quotient set constructs $\mathbb{Z}$ from the
ground up.
